# Pack authoring guide, version 4

This is for mutation testing, the software testing technique that measures
how well a project's own test suite detects small deliberate changes to its
code. Each changed copy is run only against that project's tests in an
isolated checkout and is then discarded; nothing is deployed or executed
elsewhere. The tool that makes the changes is called the mutation engine.

The mutation engine reads one small JSON data pack per programming language.
The engine itself knows no language. It parses source files with the
tree-sitter grammar that ast-grep ships for the language. It finds the syntax
nodes the pack names and rewrites them with the templates the pack gives.

You write the pack for one language. The example packs show the format only.
Do not copy their content: node kind names, field names and tokens differ
between grammars. Two grammars may use different names for the same idea, and
one name may exist in one grammar and not in another.

The pack is checked by a machine. It checks:
- the shape and size of the pack;
- that every node kind exists in the target grammar;
- that some recorded control cases get their recorded outcome.

One wrong name makes the whole pack fail. A shorter list that is correct
scores better than a longer list that contains a single guess.

## Fields

All node kind names must be exact node type names of the tree-sitter grammar
for the target language. They must be named node types as they appear in that
grammar's node-types.json, with the same spelling and case. A name that does
not exist in the grammar makes the whole pack invalid. Field names in
`field_of` must likewise be real field names of that rule in that grammar.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `language` | The language name as ast-grep spells it, lower case |
| `comment_kinds` | Node kinds of comments. Nothing inside them is ever touched. Some grammars have a single comment kind and some have separate kinds for line and block comments; list exactly the ones that exist |
| `string_kinds` | Node kinds of string literals, including multi-part or template strings. Nothing inside them is ever touched. List the outer literal kinds, not their inner fragments |
| `unwrap_kinds` | Node kinds of a parenthesis wrapper that belongs to a statement's syntax, as in `if (x)`. When a condition is such a wrapper, the engine works on the expression inside it. Use an empty list when the language's conditional statements do not require parentheses |
| `test_attribute_markers` | Text fragments of attributes or annotations that mark test-only code inside a production file. Use an empty list when the language keeps tests in separate files |
| `test_attribute_kinds` | Node kinds of the attribute or annotation items that can stand directly in front of a declaration and carry one of the `test_attribute_markers`. Required when `test_attribute_markers` is not empty. Leave it out otherwise |
| `kinds.branch_condition.field_of` | Pairs `[statement kind, field name]`: the named field of that statement kind holds a condition that decides control flow. List the conditional statements, loop statements and conditional expressions whose grammar rule has such a field. Leave a construct out if its condition is not a named field. Never invent a field name |
| `kinds.branch_condition.returned` | `{"of", "kinds", "tokens"}`. `of` lists the node kinds of a return. `kinds` lists the node kinds of logical, comparison and negation expressions. `tokens` lists the operator tokens that make such an expression a yes-or-no value, spelled as the language spells them, including keyword operators. A returned expression of one of these kinds with one of these operators is a condition |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes` | Node kinds that signal failure to the caller: raising or throwing, returning, propagating an error |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` | Optional. Maps a node kind to text prefixes. Use it for failure signals that are ordinary calls or macros in this language and can only be told apart by how they begin. Use only prefixes that belong to the language itself or its standard library |
| `kinds.error_order.nodes` | The node kind of a conditional statement that can directly follow another one of the same kind. Always use it with `"requires_next_sibling": true` |
| `kinds.state_write.nodes` | Node kinds of assignments and in-place updates: plain, compound and increment or decrement, where these are separate kinds in the grammar |
| `kinds.state_write.call_statements` | Node kinds of a call that can stand alone as a statement. Where the language has an awaited call, also list the awaited call's kind. Such a statement counts as a write made through a call |
| `kinds.pure_shell_boundary.nodes` | Node kinds of function and method definitions. Do not list anonymous function expressions unless they are the language's main way to define functions |
| `noop_statement` | Text of a statement that does nothing and is valid wherever a statement may stand. Examples are an empty statement, a pass keyword or an empty block, whichever the language accepts in every statement position |
| `statement_wrappers` | Node kinds that wrap an expression to make it a statement of its own. Use an empty list if the grammar puts expressions directly in statement position |
| `statement_terminator` | The token that ends a simple statement, if the language requires one. Leave it out for languages where line ends finish statements |

Optional `gaps` entries record constructs whose effects the tests cannot see. Each entry has a `reason` and a `nodes_with_prefix` map. Add one only for a generic language-level mechanism, such as reflection or starting a thread, whose node kind and prefix you are sure of. Otherwise leave `gaps` out.

## Operators

`operators` tells the engine how to rewrite a site. Templates may use these
placeholders:
- `{text}`: the node's text;
- `{noop}`: the `noop_statement`;
- `{child0}`: the text of the node's first named child.

| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `operators.branch_condition.template` | Replaces a condition by its logical negation. The result must be valid syntax in the place where the condition stood, for any condition expression. Always put parentheses around `{text}` so that operator precedence cannot change its meaning. Use the language's own negation operator or keyword, with a space after a keyword |
| `operators.branch_condition.token_swaps` | Pairs of operator tokens that can replace each other without changing the type of the expression: equal and not equal, a strict and a non-strict comparison, logical and and or. Spell them exactly as the language does. If the language has several spellings, for example strict and loose equality or symbolic and keyword logic operators, swap each spelling only with its own counterpart |
| `operators.branch_condition.negation_swaps` | The pairs among `token_swaps` whose swap gives exactly the logical negation of the comparison: equal and not equal, in every spelling the language has. The engine uses it to avoid producing the same change twice. Every pair here must also appear in `token_swaps`. Do not list a strict and a non-strict comparison, or and and or |
| `operators.branch_condition.exclude_kinds` | Optional. Node kinds that can appear in a condition position but cannot be negated by the template, such as a pattern-binding condition, a declaration used as a condition, or an empty condition. Include it only if such kinds really exist in the grammar |
| `operators.failure_state.by_kind` | Maps a node kind to a replacement template that removes the failure. Use `{noop}` for a statement that can simply be dropped, such as a throw or raise statement. Leave out kinds for which no replacement is valid in general, such as returning a value. Leave out expression-level kinds whose removal would leave a hole in an expression. Use `{}` when no kind qualifies |
| `operators.failure_state.returned_literal_swaps` | Pairs of literals that can replace each other as a returned value: the two boolean literals as the language spells them, and 0 and 1 |
| `operators.state_write` | Always `{"statement": "{noop}"}`: a write that is a statement of its own is replaced by the empty statement |
| `operators.error_order` | Always `{"swap_next": true}` |

## Method

Work through these steps silently before you write the pack.

1. Recall the target grammar's node types. Think of how the grammar parses a small program that contains these constructs:
   - an if/else;
   - a loop;
   - a conditional expression, if the language has one;
   - a return of a comparison;
   - a throw or raise, or an error propagation;
   - an assignment, a compound assignment and an increment;
   - a call used as a statement;
   - a function and a method;
   - comments and strings.
2. For each construct, write down the exact node type name and, for conditions, the exact field name. Watch for kinds that differ only by a prefix or suffix, and for statement forms versus expression forms. Use the form that actually occurs in that position.
3. Drop every name you are not confident exists. Omitting an optional entry is always safe. A wrong entry never is.
4. Check every template against the language's syntax:
   - The negation template must parse in a condition position, with or without surrounding parentheses.
   - `noop_statement` must parse wherever a statement can stand.
5. Check consistency:
   - `negation_swaps` must be a subset of `token_swaps`.
   - `test_attribute_kinds` must be present only if markers are present.
   - `unwrap_kinds` must be empty if conditions are unparenthesized.
   - `statement_terminator` must be absent if the language has none.

## Rules

- Be precise rather than broad: a wrong kind produces changes that do not
  parse or do not compile, and a nonexistent kind invalidates the pack.
- Do not include anything specific to a particular project, library or file.
- Keep the pack small: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters, formatted like
  the examples. Put short lists on one line.
- Use valid JSON only: double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas.

## Output

Return only the JSON object of the pack, with no text before or after it and
no code fences.

# Pack authoring guide, version 3

This is for mutation testing, the software testing technique that measures
how well a project's own test suite detects small deliberate changes to its
code. Each changed copy is run only against that project's tests in an
isolated checkout and is then discarded; nothing is deployed or executed
elsewhere. The tool that makes the changes is called the mutation engine.

You are a language tooling engineer who knows the tree-sitter grammars that
ast-grep ships, node type by node type and field by field. You write packs
that a mechanical validator accepts on the first try.

The mutation engine reads one small JSON data pack per programming language.
The engine itself knows no language. It parses source files with the
tree-sitter grammar that ast-grep ships for the language, finds syntax nodes
the pack names, and rewrites them with the templates the pack gives. You
write the pack for one language. You are given packs for other languages as
examples of the format, not as content to copy: node kind names differ
between grammars.

The pack is checked mechanically for:
1. Shape: the same keys and nesting as the examples, valid JSON.
2. Size: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters.
3. Grammar validity: every node kind and field name exists in the target
   grammar. One invented name fails the whole pack.
4. Control cases: known code snippets must be found or ignored, and mutated
   into valid code, as recorded.

## Fields

All node kind names must be exact node type names of the tree-sitter grammar
for the target language. A name that does not exist in the grammar makes the
whole pack invalid. Use the grammar's own spelling, not the language
specification's terminology or a name borrowed from another grammar.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `language` | The language name as ast-grep spells it, lower case |
| `comment_kinds` | Node kinds of comments. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `string_kinds` | Node kinds of string literals, including multi-part or template strings. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `unwrap_kinds` | Node kinds of a parenthesis wrapper that belongs to a statement's syntax, as in `if (x)`. When a condition is such a wrapper, the engine works on the expression inside it. Empty when conditions are not wrapped |
| `test_attribute_markers` | Text fragments of attributes or annotations that mark test-only code inside a production file. Empty when the language keeps tests in separate files |
| `test_attribute_kinds` | Node kinds of the attribute or annotation items that can stand directly in front of a declaration and carry one of the `test_attribute_markers`. Required when `test_attribute_markers` is not empty; leave it out otherwise |
| `kinds.branch_condition.field_of` | Pairs `[statement kind, field name]`: the named field of that statement kind holds a condition that decides control flow. List the conditional and loop statements and conditional expressions whose grammar rule has such a field |
| `kinds.branch_condition.returned` | `{"of", "kinds", "tokens"}`: `of` lists the node kinds of a return; `kinds` the node kinds of logical, comparison and negation expressions; `tokens` the operator tokens that make such an expression a yes-or-no value. A returned expression of one of these kinds with one of these operators is a condition |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes` | Node kinds that signal failure to the caller: raising or throwing, returning, propagating an error |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` | Optional. Node kind mapped to text prefixes, for failure signals that are ordinary calls or macros in this language and can only be told apart by how they begin |
| `kinds.error_order.nodes` | The node kind of a conditional statement that can directly follow another one of the same kind. Always with `"requires_next_sibling": true` |
| `kinds.state_write.nodes` | Node kinds of assignments and in-place updates |
| `kinds.state_write.call_statements` | Node kinds of a call, and of an awaited call where the language has one, that can stand alone as a statement. Such a statement counts as a write made through a call |
| `kinds.pure_shell_boundary.nodes` | Node kinds of function and method definitions |
| `noop_statement` | Text of a statement that does nothing and is valid wherever a statement may stand |
| `statement_wrappers` | Node kinds that wrap an expression to make it a statement of its own |
| `statement_terminator` | The token that ends a simple statement, if the language has one; leave it out otherwise |

Notes on fields:
- `field_of` needs a real field name declared on that rule in the grammar
  (often something like "condition"). Do not list a statement whose condition
  is an unnamed child, and do not list a loop whose header has no condition
  field.
- `unwrap_kinds` is non-empty only if the grammar actually gives the
  parenthesized condition its own node kind. If parentheses are optional or
  absent in the language's conditionals, keep it empty.
- If assignments in the grammar are statements rather than expressions,
  list the statement kind; if a separate kind exists for compound or
  augmented assignment, or for increment and decrement, list it too.
- Only list a statement wrapper that really exists in the grammar. If calls
  stand directly as statements, the list may be empty.
- `noop_statement` must be valid inside any block: an empty statement token
  in terminator languages, a pass-style keyword or an empty literal
  elsewhere.
- The examples may contain extra keys such as `gaps`. Include them only if you
  are certain every node kind and prefix inside is valid and generic;
  otherwise omit them.

## Operators

`operators` tells the engine how to rewrite a site. Templates may use
`{text}` (the node's text), `{noop}` (the `noop_statement`) and `{child0}`
(the text of the node's first named child).

| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `operators.branch_condition.template` | Replaces a condition by its logical negation. The result must be valid syntax in the place where the condition stood, for any condition expression |
| `operators.branch_condition.token_swaps` | Pairs of operator tokens that can replace each other without changing the type of the expression: equal and not equal, a strict and a non-strict comparison, logical and and or. Spell them exactly as the language does |
| `operators.branch_condition.negation_swaps` | The pairs among `token_swaps` whose swap gives exactly the logical negation of the comparison: equal and not equal, in every spelling the language has. The engine uses it to avoid producing the same change twice. Do not list a strict and a non-strict comparison, or and and or |
| `operators.branch_condition.exclude_kinds` | Optional. Node kinds that can appear in a condition position but cannot be negated by the template, such as a pattern-binding condition or an empty condition |
| `operators.failure_state.by_kind` | Node kind mapped to a replacement template that removes the failure. Use `{noop}` for a statement that can simply be dropped. Leave out kinds for which no replacement is valid in general, such as returning a value |
| `operators.failure_state.returned_literal_swaps` | Pairs of literals that can replace each other as a returned value: the two boolean literals, and 0 and 1 |
| `operators.state_write` | Always `{"statement": "{noop}"}`: a write that is a statement of its own is replaced by the empty statement |
| `operators.error_order` | Always `{"swap_next": true}` |

Notes on operators:
- Negation template: use the language's own negation operator or keyword,
  and always parenthesize `{text}` so precedence cannot change meaning. If
  the language's conditions must be wrapped in parentheses and the engine
  unwraps them, the template still only needs to produce a valid expression.
- Spell tokens exactly: word operators stay words, symbol operators stay
  symbols, in the case the language uses. Include every equality spelling
  (strict and loose identity, if both exist) in `negation_swaps`.
- Boolean literals must be spelled as the language spells them.
- In `by_kind`, map a throw or raise statement to `{noop}` only if it is a
  statement that can be dropped. If a failure signal is an expression, or
  dropping it leaves a block or function invalid, leave it out.
- Every kind used in `by_kind` or `exclude_kinds` must also be a real grammar
  kind.

## Rules

- Be precise rather than broad: a wrong kind produces changes that do not
  parse or do not compile.
- Do not include anything specific to a particular project, library or file.
- Keep the pack small: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters, formatted like
  the examples.
- When unsure whether a kind exists, leave it out; an omission costs little,
  an invented name fails everything.
- Before answering, check silently: every kind and field name is real in the
  target grammar; each template yields parseable code in its position;
  `negation_swaps` is a subset of `token_swaps`; required "Always" values are
  exact; optional keys with nothing in them are omitted rather than empty
  when the guide says to leave them out.

## Output

Return only the JSON object of the pack, with no text before or after it.
